### 4.4. Angular Momentum

We now discuss an invariant of broken lines in rank $2$ scattering diagrams that will help us distinguish which broken lines cross the Badlands. Suppose that we are considering the set of compatible pairs corresponding to a monomial $X_{1}^{p_{1}}X_{2}^{p_{2}}$ in the cluster variable $X_{n}$ .

#### Definition 4.10.

Fix a point $(q_{1},q_{2})$ on the linear portion with slope $(m_{1},m_{2})$ of a broken line terminating in the first quadrant. The angular momentum of the broken line at that point is the quantity $q_{2}m_{1}-q_{1}m_{2}$ .

#### Lemma 4.11 ([7, Lemma 5.3]).

The angular momentum is constant on a broken line.

We will be primarily interested in whether the angular momentum is positive or negative. The terminal exponent of a broken line can sometimes determine the sign of its angular momentum, and otherwise its sign also depends on the choice of terminal point.

#### Lemma 4.12.

Let $\gamma$ be a broken line in $\mathfrak{D}_{r}$ terminating at $(q_{1},q_{2})$ in the first quadrant that contributes to the monomial $X_{1}^{-c_{n-1}+rb}X_{2}^{-c_{n-2}+ra}$ in the quantum cluster variable $X_{n}$ . Then

- (1) if $rb\geq c_{n-1}$ , the angular momentum of $\gamma$ is positive,

- (2) if $ra\geq c_{n-2}$ , the angular momentum of $\gamma$ is negative,

- (3) otherwise, the angular momentum of $\gamma$ can be either positive, zero, or negative depending on the choice of $(q_{1},q_{2})$ .

#### Proof.

Since $q_{1},q_{2}>0$ , this implies that in cases (1) and (2), the angular momentum is never $0$ . The claims about the corresponding signs in cases (1) and (2) follow from the signs of the terms in the formula for angular momentum. Since there are no walls in the interior of the first quadrant, it follows that $m_{1}=-c_{n-1}+rb$ and $m_{2}=-c_{n-2}+ra$ cannot both be positive. Thus, case 3 handles when both $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are negative, in which case choosing $q_{1}\gg q_{2}$ or $q_{2}\gg q_{1}$ will change the sign of the angular momentum. ∎

#### Lemma 4.13 ([7, Lemma 5.4]).

Let $\gamma$ be a broken line in $\mathfrak{D}_{r}$ terminating in the first quadrant. If $\gamma$ has positive (resp. negative) angular momentum, then the slope of the linear portions of $\gamma$ decreases (resp. increases) at each bend, except possibly at the boundary of the first quadrant.

#### Remark 4.14.

It follows that a broken line with initial exponent $(m_{1},m_{2})$ will only bend at walls of slope less than (resp. greater than) $\frac{m_{2}}{m_{1}}$ if the broken line has negative (resp. positive) angular momentum. Thus, $\gamma$ is a broken line with negative angular momentum associated to a cluster monomial in $\mathfrak{D}_{r}$ , then $\gamma$ only bends at walls above the Badlands.

#### Definition 4.15.

Suppose we have integers $\ell_{i}\geq 0$ and $m_{i}\geq 1$ for each $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ , where the $\ell_{i}$ are decreasing. Let $\ell$ be the sequence $[(\ell_{1},m_{1}),(\ell_{2},m_{2}),\dots,(\ell_{k},m_{k})]$ . Let $\mathcal{L}^{-}_{r,n}[\ell]=\mathcal{L}^{-}_{r,n}[(\ell_{1},m_{1}),(\ell_{2},m_{2}),\dots,(\ell_{k},m_{k})]$ be the broken line in $\mathfrak{D}_{r}$ with initial slope $(-c_{n-1},-c_{n-2})$ that bends at the wall of slope $\frac{c_{\ell_{i}}}{c_{\ell_{i}+1}}$ with multiplicity $m_{i}$ and terminates at $(q_{1},q_{2})$ . By convention, the wall of slope $\frac{-1}{0}$ or $\frac{1}{0}$ is the $y$ -axis.

Similarly, let $\mathcal{L}^{+}_{r,n}[\ell]=\mathcal{L}^{+}_{r,n}[(\ell_{1},m_{1}),(\ell_{2},m_{2}),\dots,(\ell_{k},m_{k})]$ be the broken line in $\mathfrak{D}_{r}$ with initial slope $(-c_{n-1},-c_{n-2})$ that bends at the wall of slope $\frac{c_{\ell_{i}+1}}{c_{\ell_{i}}}$ with multiplicity $m_{i}$ and terminates at $(q_{1},q_{2})$ . Note that $\mathcal{L}^{-}_{r,n}[\ell]$ has negative angular momentum while $\mathcal{L}^{+}_{r,n}[\ell]$ has positive angular momentum. When $r=2$ , we additionally consider broken lines of the form $\mathcal{L}^{+}_{r,n}[(\infty,m_{\infty}),(\ell_{1},m_{1}),(\ell_{2},m_{2}),\dots,(\ell_{k},m_{k})]$ , where the broken line bends over the wall of slope $1=\lim_{\ell\to\infty}\frac{c_{\ell+1}}{c_{\ell}}$ with multiplicity $m_{\infty}$ .

The blue broken line in Figure 5 is $\mathcal{L}^{-}_{2,14}[(3,1),(2,1),(0,2)]$ , and the red broken line is $\mathcal{L}^{+}_{2,14}[(\infty,1),(2,1),(0,3)]$ .

## 5. Weights of Broken Lines

### 5.1. The Cluster Variable Case

For any integer $r$ , and for any real numbers $\alpha,\beta$ , let $f^{r}_{\alpha,\beta}$ denote the sequence where $f^{r}_{\alpha,\beta}(0)=\alpha$ , $f^{r}_{\alpha,\beta}(1)=\beta$ , and $f^{r}_{\alpha,\beta}(k+1)=rf^{r}_{\alpha,\beta}(k)-f^{r}_{\alpha,\beta}(k-1)$ for $k\geq 1$ .

#### Lemma 5.1.

For any $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and real numbers $\alpha,\beta$ , we have

$$ c_{k+1}\beta-c_{k}\alpha=f^{r}_{\alpha,\beta}(k) $$

#### Proof.

Let $g(k)=c_{k+1}\beta-c_{k}\alpha$ . We first see that

$$ \displaystyle g(k) \displaystyle=(rc_{k}-c_{k-1})\beta-(rc_{k-1}-c_{k-2})\alpha \displaystyle=r(c_{k}\beta-c_{k-1}\alpha)-(c_{k-1}\beta-c_{k-2}\alpha) \displaystyle=rg(k-1)-g(k-2)\,. $$

Moreover, we have $g(0)=\alpha$ and $g(1)=\beta$ , so we can conclude $g(k)=f^{r}_{\alpha,\beta}(k)$ . ∎

#### Corollary 5.2.

For any $n\geq\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ , we have

$$ c_{n}c_{\ell+1}-c_{n+1}c_{\ell}=c_{n-\ell+1} $$

and

$$ c_{n+1}c_{\ell+1}-c_{n}c_{\ell}=c_{n+\ell}\,. $$

#### Proof.

For the first statement, apply 5.1 with $\alpha=c_{h+1}$ and $\beta=c_{h}$ . It is then straightforward to check that $f^{r}_{c_{h+1},c_{h}}(\ell)=c_{h-\ell+1}$ .

For the second statement, apply 5.1 with $\alpha=c_{h}$ and $\beta=c_{h+1}$ . It is then straightforward to check that $f^{r}_{c_{h},c_{h+1}}(\ell)=c_{h+\ell}$ . ∎

#### Proposition 5.3.

The quantum weight of the broken line $\mathcal{L}^{-}_{r,n+2}[(\ell_{1},m_{1}),\dots,(\ell_{k},m_{k})]$ is

$$ \prod_{i=1}^{k}\binom{c_{n-\ell_{i}+1}-r\sum_{j<i}m_{\ell_{j}}c_{\ell_{j}-\ell_{i}+1}}{m_{i}}_{q^{2r}}\,. $$

#### Proof.

We prove this by induction on the number of crossings. Note that the broken line $\mathcal{L}^{-}_{r,n}[(\ell_{1},m_{1}),\dots,(\ell_{k-1},m_{k-1})]$ has terminal exponent

$$ \left(-c_{n+1}+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}m_{j}c_{\ell_{j}+1},-c_{n}+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}m_{j}c_{\ell_{j}}\right)\,. $$

Using 5.2, we can calculate that the dot product of this terminal exponent and the primitive normal vector to the wall of slope $\frac{c_{\ell_{k}}}{c_{\ell_{k}+1}}$ is $d\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}c_{n-\ell_{k}+1}-r\sum_{j<k}m_{\ell_{j}}c_{\ell_{j}-\ell_{k}+1}$ . The desired formula is then readily calculated by multiplying the quantum weight of $\mathcal{L}^{-}_{r,n+2}[(\ell_{1},m_{1}),\dots,(\ell_{k-1},m_{k-1})]$ by the binomial coefficient $\binom{d}{m_{k}}_{q^{2r}}$ . ∎

#### Remark 5.4.

In the above statement, $m_{1}$ is the multiplicity of the bending of $\gamma$ at the $y$ -axis.

#### Proposition 5.5.

The quantum weight of the broken line $\mathcal{L}^{+}_{r,n+2}[(\ell_{1},m_{1}),\dots,(\ell_{k},m_{k})]$ is

$$ \prod_{i=1}^{k}\binom{c_{n+\ell_{i}}-r\sum_{j<i}m_{\ell_{j}}c_{\ell_{j}-\ell_{i}}}{m_{i}}_{q^{2r}}\,. $$

#### Proof.

This follows from a similar argument to that for 5.3, except using the second equality in 5.2 rather than the first. ∎

#### Definition 5.6.

Let $\BL(\ell,h,a,b)$ be the collection of broken lines with initial exponent $(-\ell,-h)$ and terminal exponent $(-\ell+rb,-h+ra)$ . Let $\BL_{-}(\ell,h,a,b)$ (resp. $\BL_{+}(\ell,h,a,b)$ ) be the set of broken lines in $\BL(\ell,h,a,b)$ with negative (resp. positive) angular momentum.

Given a set of broken lines $B$ , let $|B|_{q}$ denote the sum of the weights of the broken lines in $B$ . We define $|B|\in\mathbb{Z}$ to be the value of $|B|_{q}$ under the substitution $q=1$ .

#### Lemma 5.7.

If $rb\leq c_{n}$ , we have that

$$ |\BL_{-}(c_{n+1},c_{n},a,b)|_{q}=\sum_{t=0}^{a}\binom{c_{n+1}-rb}{t}_{q^{2r}}|\BL_{-}(c_{n},c_{n-1},r(a-t)-b,a-t)|_{q} $$

#### Proof.

Fix a broken line $\gamma=\mathcal{L}^{-}_{r,n+2}[(\ell_{1},m_{1}),\dots,(\ell_{k},m_{k})]$ in $\BL_{-}(c_{n+1},c_{n},a,b)$ . Let $t$ denote the multiplicity of the crossing over the $y$ -axis, i.e., $t=m_{k}$ if $\ell_{k}=0$ and $t=0$ otherwise. If $t=0$ , let $\gamma^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}^{-}_{r,n+1}[(\ell_{1}-1,m_{1}),\dots,(\ell_{k-1}-1,m_{k-1})]$ , and otherwise let $\gamma^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}^{-}_{r,n+1}[(\ell_{1}-1,m_{1}),\dots,(\ell_{k}-1,m_{k})]$ . Note that we have $\gamma^{\prime}\in\BL_{-}(c_{n},c_{n-1},r(a-t)-b,a-t)$ . By 5.3, we have $|\gamma|_{q}=\binom{c_{n+1}-rb}{t}_{q}|\gamma^{\prime}|_{q}$ . Note that the map from $\gamma$ to $\gamma^{\prime}$ is bijective (considered as a map on unweighted broken lines). Therefore, summing over all choices of $\gamma$ in $\BL_{-}(c_{n+1},c_{n},a,b)$ yields the desired equality. ∎

### 5.2. The Kronecker Case

We first handle broken lines of positive angular momentum and then broken lines of initial exponent $(-h,-h)$ . The latter are the broken lines corresponding to the theta basis elements of $\mathcal{A}_{q}(2,2)$ that are not cluster monomials.

#### Proposition 5.8.

In the Kronecker scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{2}$ , the quantum weight of the broken line $\mathcal{L}^{+}_{r,n+2}[(\infty,m_{\infty}),(\ell_{1},m_{1}),\dots,(\ell_{k},m_{k})]$ is

$$ [m_{\infty}+1]_{q^{4}}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\binom{(n+\ell_{i}-2m_{\infty})-2\sum_{j<i}m_{\ell_{j}}(\ell_{j}-\ell_{i})}{m_{i}}_{q^{4}}\,. $$

#### Lemma 5.9.

In the Kronecker scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{2}$ , we have that

$$ |\BL_{+}(h+1,h,a,b)|_{q}=\sum_{t=0}^{b}\binom{h-2a}{t}_{q^{4}}|\BL_{+}(h,h-1,b-t,2(b-t)-a)|_{q} $$

whenever $2a\leq h+1$ .

#### Proof.

Fix a broken line $\gamma=\mathcal{L}^{+}_{r,h+3}[(\infty,m_{\infty}),(\ell_{1},m_{1}),\dots,(\ell_{k},m_{k})]$ in $\BL_{-}(h+1,h,a,b)$ . Let $t$ denote the multiplicity of the crossing over the $x$ -axis, i.e., $t=m_{k}$ if $\ell_{k}=0$ and $t=0$ otherwise. If $t=0$ , let $\gamma^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}^{+}_{r,h+2}[(\infty,m_{\infty}),(\ell_{1}-1,m_{1}),\dots,(\ell_{k-1}-1,m_{k-1})]$ , and otherwise let $\gamma^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}^{+}_{r,h+2}[(\infty,m_{\infty}),(\ell_{1}-1,m_{1}),\dots,(\ell_{k}-1,m_{k})]$ . Note that we have $\gamma^{\prime}\in\BL_{-}(h,h-1,b-t,2(b-t)-a)$ . By 5.8, we have $|\gamma|_{q}=\binom{c_{h}-2b}{t}_{q}|\gamma^{\prime}|_{q}$ . Note that the map from $\gamma$ to $\gamma^{\prime}$ is bijective (considered as a map on unweighted broken lines). Therefore, summing over all choices of $\gamma$ in $\BL_{-}(h+1,h,a,b)$ yields the desired equality. ∎

#### Proposition 5.10.

Suppose $r=2$ and $2b\leq h$ . The quantum weight of the broken line in $\BL_{-}(h,h,a,b)$ crossing at the wall $\mathfrak{d}_{\ell_{i}/(\ell_{i}+1)}$ with multiplicity $m_{i}$ for $\ell_{1}>\cdots>\ell_{k}\geq-1$ is

$$ \prod_{i=1}^{k}\binom{h-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}2m_{j}(\ell_{i}-\ell_{j})}{m_{i}}_{q^{4}}\,. $$

#### Proof.

Denote this broken line by $\gamma$ . Let $p_{i}$ be the exponent of $\gamma$ after bending at the wall $\mathfrak{d}_{\ell_{i}/(\ell_{i}+1)}$ , and let $p_{0}=(-h,-h)$ . It is straightforward to prove by induction that we have

$$ p_{i}=\left(-h+2\sum_{j=-1}^{i}m_{j}\ell_{j},-h+2\sum_{j=-1}^{i}m_{j}(\ell_{j}+1)\right)\, $$

Thus, the dot product of $p_{i-1}$ with the primitive normal vector to the wall $\mathfrak{d}_{\ell_{i}/(\ell_{i}+1)}$ is

$$ p_{i-1}\cdot(-\ell_{i},\ell_{i}+1)=h-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}2m_{j}(\ell_{j}-\ell_{i})\,. $$

The weight of the broken line is then the product of quantum binomial coefficients $\binom{p_{i-1}\cdot(-\ell_{i},\ell_{i}+1)}{m_{i}}_{q^{4}}$ . ∎

#### Lemma 5.11.

If $r=2$ and $2b\leq h$ , we have that

$$ |\BL_{-}(h,h,a,b)|_{q}=\sum_{t=0}^{a}\binom{h-2b}{t}_{q^{4}}|\BL_{-}(h,h,2(a-t)-b,a-t)|_{q}\,. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is essentially the same as that of 5.9, but adapted for the initial exponent $(-h,-h)$ . Consider the broken line $\gamma\in\BL_{-}(h,h,a,b)$ that bends over the wall $\frac{\ell-1}{\ell}$ with multiplicity $m_{\ell}$ for $\ell\geq 0$ . Let $m_{0}=t$ . We then map $\gamma$ to $\gamma^{\prime}\in|\BL_{-}(h,h,2(a-t)-b,a-t)|$ that bends over the wall $\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}$ with multiplicity $m_{\ell}$ for $\ell\geq 0$ . By 5.10, we can see that $w_{q}(\gamma)=\binom{h-2b}{t}_{q^{4}}w_{q}(\gamma^{\prime})$ . The desired equality follows from summing over all possible values of $m_{0}=t$ . ∎

## 6. A Bijection for $r$ -Kronecker Cluster Monomials

### 6.1. Construction of the Bijection

We now construct a $q$ -weighted bijection between positive compatible pairs and broken lines of negative angular momentum associated to quantum cluster monomials in the $r$ -Kronecker cluster algebra. That is, for $\ell\geq rb$ , we construct a map $\varphi:\CP(\ell,h,a,b)\to\BL_{-}(\ell,h,a,b)$ such that, for a broken line $\gamma\in\BL_{-}(\ell,h,a,b)$ , we have

$$ \sum_{(S_{1},S_{2})\in\varphi^{-1}(\gamma)}w_{q}(S_{1},S_{2})=|\gamma|_{q}\,. $$

#### Definition 6.1.

A vertical edge $\nu$ is overshadowing if the horizontal edge shadow-paired with $\nu$ is in $S_{1}$ . A vertical edge $\nu$ is overflowing if the horizontal edge cascade-paired with $\nu$ is in $S_{1}$ .

We say that a vertical edge of $\mathcal{P}$ is protruding if it has fewer than $r$ horizontal edges to its immediate left. Note that, by the compatibility condition, if a vertical edge is overshadowing or overflowing, then it is protruding. We denote the protruding edges of $\mathcal{P}$ by $\nu_{\pro,1},\dots,\nu_{\pro,rh-\ell}$ , ordered from bottom to top.

Suppose $(r-1)h\leq\ell\leq rh$ . Let $\ell^{\prime}=h$ and $h^{\prime}=rh-\ell$ , and consider the paths $\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}(\ell,h)$ and $\mathcal{P}^{\prime}=\mathcal{P}(\ell^{\prime},h^{\prime})$ . Note that the path $\mathcal{P}^{\prime}$ is obtained from $\mathcal{P}$ by replacing the sequence of steps $E^{r-1}N$ with $EN$ and $E^{r}N$ with $E$ .

#### Definition 6.2.

We define a map $\ttheta:\CP(\mathcal{P})\to\CP(\mathcal{P})$ taking $(S_{1},S_{2})$ to $(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2})$ , where

- • $\widetilde{S}_{1}=\{\eta_{i}\in\mathcal{P}^{\prime}:\nu_{i}\in\mathcal{P}\cut S_{2}\}$ , and

- • $\widetilde{S}_{2}=\{\nu_{j}\in\mathcal{P}^{\prime}:\nu_{\pro,j}\text{ is overflowing}\}$

#### Remark 6.3.

It is not clear from the definition that the resulting set of edges in the image of $\ttheta$ is a compatible pair. This fact is proven in 6.8. Moreover, when restricted to the set $\CP_{\cas}(\ell,h,a,b)$ , the map $\ttheta$ yields a compatible pair in $\CP(\ell^{\prime},h^{\prime},h-b,a)$ .

Let $(S_{1}^{(i)},S_{2}^{(i)})=\underbrace{\ttheta\circ\ttheta\circ\cdots\circ\ttheta}_{i}(S_{1},S_{2})$ for $i\geq 0$ . Let $b_{i}=|S_{2}^{(i)}|$ . Note that the sequence $b_{i}$ is weakly decreasing, and we have $b_{i}=0$ for sufficiently large $i$ .

#### Definition 6.4.

Let $\mathcal{P}(\ell,h)$ be a Dyck path corresponding to a cluster monomial. We define $\varphi:\CP(\ell,h,a,b)\to\BL_{-}(\ell,h,a,b)$ to be the map taking a compatible pair $(S_{1},S_{2})$ to the broken line that crosses the wall of slope $\frac{c_{i}}{c_{i-1}}$ with multiplicity $b_{i-1}-(rb_{i}-b_{i+1})$ .

A potential direction for further work would be extending this bijection to all broken lines that arise in the theta bases of rank- $2$ (quantum) cluster algebras. This problem was posed in the classical case in [7, Remark 3.6], as this would give a combinatorial proof that the greedy and theta bases coincide. In the quantum setting, it is not yet known if these bases coincide, though this was suggested to be true in [9, Section 1.4]. For the quantum Kronecker cluster algebra, we show at the end of Section 7 that the quantum greedy and theta bases indeed coincide.

### 6.2. Proof of Compatibility

We begin by recalling a map $\theta$ that takes a compatible pair to another compatible pair on a different Dyck path. This map originally appeared in the work of Lee–Li–Zelevinsky and was used in their proof of 2.5.

#### Definition 6.5 ([19, Lemma 3.5]).

If $(r-1)h\leq\ell\leq rh$ , then the map $\theta:\CP_{\cas}(\ell,h,a,b)\to\CP(\ell^{\prime},h^{\prime},h-b,a)$ taking $(S_{1},S_{2})$ to $(S_{1}^{\prime},S_{2}^{\prime})$ is defined as follows:

- • $S_{1}^{\prime}=\{\eta_{i}\in\mathcal{P}^{\prime}:\nu_{h+1-i}\text{ is overshadowing}\}$ , and

- • $S_{2}^{\prime}=\{\nu_{j}\in\mathcal{P}^{\prime}:\nu_{j}\in\mathcal{P}\cut S_{2}\}$ .

#### Remark 6.6.

Our definition of the Lee-Li-Zelevinsky map $\theta$ differs from their original formulation. Moreover, we apply $\theta$ to compatible pairs (rather than sets of horizontal edges). It is straightforward to show that the two definitions are equivalent (up to conjugating the underlying Dyck path and including the vertical edges).

We now prove that any set of edges $(S_{1},S_{2})$ in the image of $\widetilde{\theta}$ is indeed a compatible pair. To do this, we utilize that the map $\theta$ has this property.

#### Theorem 6.7.

We have $\theta(S_{1},S_{2})=(\ttheta\circ\lambda)(S_{1},S_{2})$ for any $(S_{1},S_{2})\in\CP_{\sh}(\ell,h,a,b)$ .

#### Proof.

Note that $\lambda$ does not affect $S_{2}$ and both $\theta$ and $\ttheta$ replace $S_{2}$ with its complement. The map $\theta$ depends on which edges of $S_{2}$ are overshadowing in $(S_{1},S_{2})$ , while the map $\ttheta$ depends analogously on which edges of $S_{2}$ are overflowing in $\lambda(S_{1},S_{2})$ . By 3.11, the overshadowing edges of $(S_{1},S_{2})$ coincide with the overflowing edges of $\lambda(S_{1},S_{2})$ . Therefore, we can conclude that the maps are the same. ∎

#### Corollary 6.8.

For compatible pairs on Dyck paths corresponding to cluster monomials, the map $\ttheta$ preserves compatibility.

#### Proof.

By 3.9, the map $\lambda^{-1}$ preserves compatibility for the cluster monomials (which includes the setting in which $\ttheta$ is defined). By 6.7, we have $\ttheta=\theta\circ\lambda^{-1}$ . Since the map $\theta$ preserves compatibility (see [19, Lemma 3.5]), we can conclude that $\ttheta$ does as well. ∎

### 6.3. Preservation of Quantum Weight

We now show that, on a path $\mathcal{P}(\ell,h)$ corresponding to a cluster monomial, the map $\ttheta$ preserves the quantum weights of compatible pairs. Thus, the map $\varphi:\CP(\ell,h,a,b)\to\BL_{-}(\ell,h,a,b)$ is a $q$ -weighted bijection (see 6.18). Throughout this section, let $(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2})=\ttheta(S_{1},S_{2})$ .

#### Proposition 6.9.

Let $\omega\in\{h,v,H,V\}^{*}$ be the word associated to a compatible pair in $\CP(\ell,h,a,b)$ where $\mathcal{P}(\ell,h)$ corresponds to a cluster monomial. If we swap an instance $h$ with an $H$ to its right such that the segment $\sigma$ between them satisfies $|\sigma_{h}|+|\sigma_{H}|=r|\sigma_{V}|$ , then the quantum weight increases by $2r$ .

#### Proof.

Note that the above expression does not take into account $|\sigma_{v}|$ . Moreover, the quantum weight contributed from portions of $\omega$ outside the segment $h\sigma H$ (or $H\sigma h$ ) are unaffected. We can then calculate that

$$ \displaystyle w_{q}(H\sigma h) \displaystyle=w_{q}(Hh)+w_{q}(|\sigma_{H}|HH+|\sigma_{V}|HV+|\sigma_{h}|Hh+|\sigma_{v}|Hv) \displaystyle\hskip 51.21504pt+w_{q}(|\sigma_{H}|Hh+|\sigma_{V}|Vh+|\sigma_{h}|hh+|\sigma_{v}|vh) \displaystyle=r+|\sigma_{V}|(1-r^{2})+|\sigma_{h}|r+|\sigma_{v}|+|\sigma_{H}|r-|\sigma_{V}|-|\sigma_{v}| \displaystyle=r+|\sigma_{V}|(1-r^{2})+(r|\sigma_{V}|-|\sigma_{H}|)r+|\sigma_{H}|r-|\sigma_{V}| \displaystyle=r $$

and

$$ \displaystyle w_{q}(h\sigma H) \displaystyle=w_{q}(hH)+w_{q}(|\sigma_{H}|hH+|\sigma_{V}|hV+|\sigma_{h}|hh+|\sigma_{v}|hv) \displaystyle\hskip 51.21504pt+w_{q}(|\sigma_{H}|HH+|\sigma_{V}|VH+|\sigma_{h}|hH+|\sigma_{v}|vH) \displaystyle=-r-|\sigma_{H}|r+|\sigma_{V}|+|\sigma_{v}|+|\sigma_{V}|(r^{2}-1)-|\sigma_{h}|r-|\sigma_{v}| \displaystyle=-r-(r|\sigma_{V}|-|\sigma_{h}|)r+|\sigma_{V}|+|\sigma_{V}|(r^{2}-1)-|\sigma_{h}|r \displaystyle=-r\,. $$

The resulting change in the quantum weight is then $w_{q}(H\sigma h-h\sigma H)=2r$ , as desired. ∎

#### Lemma 6.10.

Fix a positive compatible pair $(S_{1},S_{2})$ on $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ . Suppose that the horizontal edge $\eta_{i}\notin S_{1}$ is cascade-paired with $\nu_{j}\in S_{2}$ and that $\eta_{i}$ is to the left of $\nu_{j}$ . Then

$$ w_{q}(S_{1}\cup\{\eta_{i}\},S_{2})-w_{q}(S_{1},S_{2})=w_{q}(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2}\cup\{\nu_{j^{\prime}}\})-w_{q}(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2})\,. $$

#### Proof.

We begin by decomposing $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ into several paths. Let $p_{1}$ be the leftmost point along $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ at the same height at $\eta_{i}$ . Let $p_{2}$ be the left endpoint of $\eta_{i}$ and let $p_{3}$ be the top endpoint of $\nu_{j}$ . Let $X$ be subpath of $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ consisting of all edges below $p_{1}$ , and let $Y$ be the path from $p_{1}$ to $p_{2}$ . Let $S$ be the path from $p_{2}$ to $p_{3}$ , and let $Z$ be the subpath of $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ consisting of all edges to the right of $p_{3}$ .

We similarly decompose $\mathcal{C}_{n-1}$ into several paths. Let $\widetilde{X}$ be the image of $X$ , $\widetilde{S}$ be the image of $Y\cup\{\eta_{i}\}\cup S$ with $\nu_{j^{\prime}}$ removed, and $\widetilde{Z}$ be the image of $Z$ .

Expanding out the pairs of edges that involve $\eta_{i}$ in $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle w_{q}(S_{1}\cup\{\eta_{i}\},S_{2})-w_{q}(S_{1},S_{2}) \displaystyle=w_{q}(XYHSZ-XYhSZ) \displaystyle=r|S+Z-X-Y|_{h,H}+r^{2}|X+Y-S-Z|_{V} $$

and

$$ w_{q}(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2}\cup\{\eta_{j}\})-w_{q}(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2})=r|\widetilde{X}+\widetilde{S}-\widetilde{Z}|_{v,V}+r^{2}|\widetilde{Z}-\widetilde{X}-\widetilde{S}|_{H}\,. $$

Thus, we want to show that the quantity

$$ \displaystyle\alpha \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}r\left(|S+Z-X-Y|_{h,H}+|\widetilde{Z}-\widetilde{X}-\widetilde{S}|_{v,V}\right) \displaystyle\qquad+r^{2}\left(|X+Y-S-Z|_{V}+|\widetilde{X}+\widetilde{S}-\widetilde{Z}|_{H}\right) $$

vanishes. By the definition of the map $\rho$ , we have

$$ r|X|_{v,V}-|X|_{h,H}=|\widetilde{X}|_{v,V}\text{ and }r|Z|_{v,V}-|Z|_{h,H}=|\widetilde{Z}|_{v,V}\,. $$

Hence

$$ r^{2}|X-Z|_{V}+r|Z-X|_{h,H}+r|\widetilde{Z}-\widetilde{X}|_{v,V}=r^{2}|Z-X|_{v}\,. $$

Plugging this into our expression for $\alpha$ , we find

$$ \displaystyle\alpha \displaystyle=r\left(|S-Y|_{h,H}-|\widetilde{S}|_{v,V}\right)+r^{2}\left(|Y-S|_{V}+|\widetilde{X}+\widetilde{S}-\widetilde{Z}|_{H}+|Z-X|_{v}\right)\,. $$

By the definition of the map $\rho$ , we have $|W|_{V}=|\widetilde{W}|_{h}$ and $|W|_{v}=|\widetilde{W}|_{H}$ for $W=X,S,Z$ . We also must have $|Y|_{v,V}=0$ . Thus, we can further simplify $\alpha$ to

$$ \displaystyle\alpha \displaystyle=r\left(|S-Y|_{h,H}-|\widetilde{S}|_{v,V}\right)+r^{2}\left(|S|_{v}-|S|_{V}\right)\,. $$

We furthermore have

$$ r|S|_{v,V}-|Y+S|_{h,H}-1=|\widetilde{S}|_{v,V}+1\,, $$

hence we have

$$ \alpha=2r|S|_{h,H}-2r^{2}|S|_{V}+2r=-2r(r|S|_{V}-|S|_{h,H}-1)\,. $$

Since the shadow of $\nu_{j}$ extends to $\eta_{i}$ , we have $r|S|_{V}-|S|_{h,H}-1=0$ . We can therefore conclude that $\alpha=0$ , as desired. ∎

#### Lemma 6.11.

Fix a positive compatible pair $(S_{1},S_{2})$ on $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ . Suppose that the horizontal edge $\eta_{i}\notin S_{1}$ is cascade-paired with $\nu_{j}\in S_{2}$ and that $\eta_{i}$ is to the right of $\nu_{j}$ . Then

$$ w_{q}(S_{1}\cup\{\eta_{i}\},S_{2})-w_{q}(S_{1},S_{2})=w_{q}(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2}\cup\{\nu_{j^{\prime}}\})-w_{q}(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2}) $$

#### Proof.

We proceed via analogous methods to the proof of 6.10. We start by decomposing $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ into several paths. Let $p_{1}$ be the left endpoint of $\eta_{i}$ and let $p_{2}$ be the right endpoint of $\eta_{i}$ . Let $p_{3}$ be the rightmost point along $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ at the same height as $\eta_{i}$ . Let $S$ be subpath of $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ consisting of all edges below $p_{1}$ , and let $Y$ be the path from $p_{1}$ to $p_{2}$ . Let $S$ be the path from $p_{2}$ to $p_{3}$ , and let $Z$ be the subpath of $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ consisting of all edges to the right of or above $p_{3}$ . Note that $\sh(\nu_{j};S_{2})=S\cup Y\cup\{\eta_{i}\}$ .

We similarly decompose $\mathcal{C}_{n-1}$ into several paths. Let $\widetilde{S}$ be the image of $S$ with $\nu_{j^{\prime}}$ removed, and let $\widetilde{Z}$ be the image of $\{\eta_{i}\}\cup Y\cup Z$ .

Expanding out the pairs of edges that involve $\eta_{i}$ in $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle w_{q}(S_{1}\cup\{\eta_{i}\},S_{2})-w_{q}(S_{1},S_{2}) \displaystyle=w_{q}(SYHZ-SYhZ) \displaystyle=r|Y+Z-S|_{h,H}+r^{2}|S-Y-Z|_{V} \displaystyle=r|Y+Z-S|_{h,H}+r^{2}|S-Z|_{V} $$

and

$$ w_{q}(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2}\cup\{\eta_{j}\})-w_{q}(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2})=r|\widetilde{S}-\widetilde{Z}|_{v,V}+r^{2}|\widetilde{Z}-\widetilde{S}|_{H}\,. $$

Thus, we want to show that the quantity

$$ \displaystyle\alpha \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}r\left(|Y+Z-S|_{h,H}+|\widetilde{Z}-\widetilde{S}|_{v,V}\right)+r^{2}\left(|S-Z|_{V}+|\widetilde{S}-\widetilde{Z}|_{H}\right) $$

vanishes.

By the definition of the map $\rho$ , we have

$$ r|S|_{v,V}-|S|_{h,H}=|\widetilde{S}|_{v,V}+1 $$

and

$$ r|Z|_{v,V}-|Y+Z|_{h,H}-1=|\widetilde{Z}|_{v,V}\,. $$

Substituting these into our expression for $\alpha$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\alpha \displaystyle=r\left(|Y+Z|_{h,H}+|\widetilde{Z}|_{v,V}\right)+r^{2}\left(-|Z|_{V}+|\widetilde{S}-\widetilde{Z}|_{H}-|S|_{v}\right)+r \displaystyle=r^{2}\left(|Z-S|_{v}+|\widetilde{S}-\widetilde{Z}|_{H}\right)\,. $$

We furthermore have that $|S|_{v}=|\widetilde{S}|_{H}$ and $|Z|_{v}=|\widetilde{Z}|_{H}$ . We can thus conclude that $\alpha=0$ , as desired. ∎

#### Lemma 6.12.

For any compatible pair $(S_{1},S_{2})$ with $S_{1}\subseteq\cas(S_{2})$ , we have

$$ w_{q}(S_{1}\cup(\mathcal{P}_{1}\cut\sh(S_{2})),S_{2})=w_{q}(S_{1},S_{2})\,. $$

#### Proof.

This follows because, for any $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , we have

$$ w_{q}(Vh+mhh+(r-m)Hh)=w_{q}(VH+mhH+(r-m)HH) $$

and $w_{q}(hv)=w_{q}(Hv)$ . ∎

#### Lemma 6.13.

If $rb\leq\ell$ and the path $\mathcal{P}(\ell,h)$ corresponds to a cluster monomial, then the restriction of the $\ttheta$ to the set $\CP_{\cas}(\ell,h,a,b)$ preserves the quantum weight of compatible pairs.

#### Proof.

We first see that $\ttheta$ preserves quantum weights when $S_{1}$ is empty, since the quantum weight of $(\emptyset,S_{2})$ only depends on the number of $i,j\in[h]$ such that $\nu_{i}\in S_{2}$ and $\nu_{j}\notin S_{1}$ . An analogous statement holds for $\ttheta(\emptyset,S_{2})=(\emptyset,\emptyset)$ .

One can then add on horizontal edges to the compatible pair one-by-one. The fact that the quantum weight is preserved under this operation follows from 6.10 and 6.11. ∎

We lastly show that the compatible pairs satisfy an analogous recursion to that for the broken lines 5.7.

#### Lemma 6.14.

If $rb\leq c_{n+1}$ , We have that

$$ |\CP(c_{n+1},c_{n},a,b)|_{q}=\sum_{t=0}^{a}\binom{c_{n+1}-rb}{t}_{q^{2r}}|\CP(c_{n},c_{n-1},r(a-t)-b,a-t)|_{q}\,. $$

#### Proof.

We first note that

$$ |\CP(c_{n+1},c_{n},,a,b)|_{q}=\bigcup_{t=0}^{a}|\{(S_{1},S_{2})\in\CP(c_{n+1},c_{n},a,b):|\cas(S_{2})\cap S_{1}|=t\}|\,. $$

Hence, by 6.9 and 6.13, we have

$$ |\CP(c_{n+1},c_{n},,a,b)|_{q}=\sum_{t=0}^{a}\binom{c_{n+1}-rb}{t}_{q^{2r}}|\CP_{\cas}(c_{n+1},c_{n},a-t,b)|_{q}\,. $$

Then, applying $\theta$ to $\CP_{\cas}(c_{n+1},c_{n},a-t,b)$ and using 6.12, we have

$$ \displaystyle|\CP_{\cas}(c_{n+1},c_{n},a-t,b)|_{q} \displaystyle=|\{(S_{1},S_{2})\in\CP(c_{n},c_{n-1},c_{n}-b,a-t):\mathcal{P}_{1}\cut\cas(S_{2})\subseteq S_{1}\}|_{q} \displaystyle=|\CP_{\cas}(c_{n},c_{n-1},r(a-t)-b,a-t)|_{q}\,. $$

The desired equality follows from substituting the above expression in the summation. ∎

### 6.4. From Cluster Variables to Cluster Monomials

The quantum analogs of cluster monomials for $\mathcal{A}_{q}(r,r)$ the bar-invariant quantum cluster monomials, which are elements in $\mathcal{T}$ of the form $q^{\alpha\beta}X_{n}^{\alpha}X_{n+1}^{\beta}$ .

While we have restricted the proofs in this section to the cluster variable case for simplicity, the same methods can be readily adapted to the case of cluster monomials. In this subsection, we outline the main steps of this adaptation to the cluster monomial case.

Let $c_{n}[\alpha,\beta]=\alpha c_{n}+\beta c_{n-1}$ . Note that the sequence $c_{n}[\alpha,\beta]$ still satisfies the recursion $c_{n+1}[\alpha,\beta]=rc_{n}[\alpha,\beta]-c_{n-1}[\alpha,\beta]$ , and that $c_{n}=c_{n}[1,0]$ .

#### Remark 6.15.

The statement and proofs of 5.2, 5.3, and 5.7 hold true if $c_{n}$ is replaced with $c_{n}[\alpha,\beta]$ whenever $n\in\{h-\ell+1,h-1,h,h+1,h+\ell\}$ . Thus, we have

$$ |\BL_{-}(c_{n+1}[\alpha,\beta],c_{n}[\alpha,\beta],a,b)|_{q}=\sum_{t=0}^{a}\binom{c_{n}[\alpha,\beta]-b}{a-t}_{q^{2r}}|\BL_{-}(c_{n}[\alpha,\beta],c_{n-1}[\alpha,\beta],rt-b,t)|_{q}\,. $$

In order to study the compatible pairs associated to cluster monomials, we first address how to construct cascades.

#### Remark 6.16.

The path $\mathcal{P}(\alpha c_{n}+\beta c_{n+1},\alpha c_{n-1}+\beta c_{n})$ can be constructed by appending copies of the paths $\mathcal{P}(c_{n},c_{n-1})$ or $\mathcal{P}(c_{n+1},c_{n})$ . Proceeding from left to right, the $i^{\text{th}}$ subpath appended is $\mathcal{P}(c_{n+1},c_{n})$ whenever the $i^{\text{th}}$ edge of $\mathcal{P}(\alpha,\beta)$ is horizontal and is $\mathcal{P}(c_{n},c_{n-1})$ otherwise.

#### Definition 6.17.

Let $\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}(\alpha c_{n}+\beta c_{n+1},\alpha c_{n-1}+\beta c_{n})$ be a maximal Dyck path corresponding to a cluster monomial in $\mathcal{A}(r,r)$ . Decompose $\mathcal{P}$ into $\alpha+\beta$ subpaths $\{\mathcal{P}_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq\alpha+\beta}$ of the form $\mathcal{P}(c_{n},c_{n-1})$ or $\mathcal{P}(c_{n+1},c_{n})$ . Then, for $S_{2}\subset\mathcal{P}_{2}$ , the cascade of $S_{2}$ is computed locally on each subpath $\mathcal{P}_{i}$ according to 3.3.

Having constructed cascades, the definition of the map $\ttheta$ can then be extended directly to the cluster monomial case. The proof that $\ttheta$ preserves quantum weights follows identically from that in Subsection 6.3 except that now cascades are considered locally on each subpath $\mathcal{P}_{i}$ . That is, one can readily check that the quantum weight is preserved for compatible pairs with no horizontal edge, and then one can iteratively add in horizontal edges using 6.10 and 6.11. From this, we can conclude

$$ |\CP(c_{n+1}[\alpha,\beta],c_{n}[\alpha,\beta],a,b)|_{q}=\sum_{t=0}^{a}\binom{c_{n}[\alpha,\beta]-a}{a-t}_{q^{2r}}|\CP(c_{n}[\alpha,\beta],c_{n-1}[\alpha,\beta],rt-b,t)|_{q}\,. $$

Combining this with 6.15, we can conclude that, in the cluster monomial setting, $\ttheta$ is a weighted bijection that preserves quantum weights. Thus, we can conclude that $\varphi$ is a $q$ -weighted bijection in the cluster monomial case.

#### Theorem 6.18.

If $rb\leq\ell$ and the path $\mathcal{P}(\ell,h)$ corresponds to a cluster monomial, then the map $\varphi:\CP(\ell,h,a,b)\to\BL_{-}(\ell,h,a,b)$ is a $q$ -weighted bijection.

#### Proof.

By the above discussion, it is enough to consider the cluster variable case. The map $\varphi$ is defined by taking successive applications of the map $\ttheta$ and extracting the associated quantum binomial coefficient, which also corresponds to a bending of a broken line at one wall of the scattering diagram. A recursion for the quantum weights of the compatible pairs in terms of $\ttheta$ is given in 6.14 that matches the recursion given for broken lines of negative angular momentum 5.7. Thus, we can conclude that $\varphi$ is a bijection that preserves quantum weights. ∎

By 2.7, 6.18 applies to almost all compatible pairs on paths corresponding to cluster monomials.

## 7. A Bijection for the Kronecker Theta Basis

In this section, we now study a map between all compatible pairs and broken lines corresponding to theta basis elements of the quantum Kronecker cluster algebra $\mathcal{A}_{q}(2,2)$ . We then show that the theta basis for the quantum Kronecker cluster algebra coincides with many other bases, including the quantum triangular, greedy, and bracelets bases.

### 7.1. Positive angular momentum

In order to handle the positive angular momentum case, we first extend our map $\ttheta$ . The fact that this map indeed preserves compatibility is shown in 7.3. We will be primarily interested in the cascade structure of $\mathcal{P}(n-3,n-2)$ , which is obtained from $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ by a reflection. Since we are working in the reflected Dyck path, we take the convention that $|S_{1}|=b$ and $|S_{2}|=a$ in this subsection.

- • $\nu_{h}\in\mathcal{P}^{\prime}$ (resp. $\nu_{h+1}\in\mathcal{P}^{\prime}$ ) is included in $\widetilde{S}_{2}$ if the horizontal edge that is $1$ -cascade-paired (resp. $2$ -cascade-paired) with $\nu_{h}\in\mathcal{P}$ is in $S_{1}$ .

#### Proposition 7.3.

If $2a\leq h-1$ , then the map $\ttheta:\CP_{\cas}(h-1,h,b,a)\to\CP(h,h+1,h-a,b)$ preserves compatibility.

Then $\nu_{j}\in S_{2}$ is overshadowing, which implies that $j=1$ or $\nu_{j-1}\in S_{2}$ . Hence, $\eta_{j}$ and $\eta_{j-1}$ are not in $\widetilde{S}_{1}$ . Moreover, if $\nu_{h}\in S_{2}$ , then $\eta_{h}\notin\widetilde{S}_{1}$ . Combining this with the characterization of compatible pairs above, we can conclude that $(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2})$ is compatible. ∎

Another distinction of the positive angular momentum case is that the size of $S_{2}$ is only non-decreasing, rather than strictly decreasing as in the negative angular momentum case. #### Proposition 7.4.

Suppose $(S_{1},S_{2})$ is a compatible pair on $\mathcal{P}(h-1,h)$ , and let $\ttheta(S_{1},S_{2})=(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2})$ If $|S_{2}|=|\widetilde{S}_{2}|$ , then $(S_{1},S_{2})$ is of the form

$$ \displaystyle S_{2} \displaystyle=\{\nu_{k}\in\mathcal{P}:k\in[1,i]\cup[h-j+1,h]\}\,. \displaystyle S_{1} \displaystyle\supset\{\eta_{k}:k\in[i+1,2i]\cup[h-2j+1,h-j]\}\,. $$

Moreover, we have that, if $\ttheta(\widetilde{S}_{1},\widetilde{S}_{2})=(S_{1}^{\prime},S_{2}^{\prime})$ , then $|S_{2}^{\prime}|=|\widetilde{S}_{2}|$ .

#### Proof.

Consider a collection $C$ of contiguous vertical edges in $S_{2}$ . If the collection does not contain $\nu_{h}$ , then $\cas(C)$ contains the horizontal edge preceding each edge in $C$ . These cannot be included $S_{1}$ , so $|\cas(C)\cap S_{1}|\leq|C|$ . Moreover, if $\nu_{j}$ is the lowest edge in $C$ for $j\geq 2$ , then $\eta_{j-1}$ must not be in $S_{1}$ in order to maintain compatibility. Hence $|S_{1}\cap\cas(C)|\leq|C|-1$ .

The only cases that were excluded in the above consideration are when $\nu_{1}$ or $\nu_{h}$ is in $C$ . In both cases, the above arguments show that $|\cas(C)\cap S_{1}|\leq|C|$ . Thus, if $|\cas(C)\cap S_{1}|\leq|C|$ , then $C$ must be a contiguous set of vertical edges at the top or bottom of $\mathcal{P}$ , and $S_{1}\cap\cas(C)$ must be maximal while maintaining the compatibility condition.

Lastly, note that if we apply $\ttheta$ to a compatible pair of this form, the resulting compatible pair is also of this form. ∎

#### Definition 7.5.

The map $\varphi$ takes the compatible pair $(S_{1},S_{2})\in\CP(h-1,h,b,a)$ to the broken line in $\BL_{+}(h,h-1,b,a)$ that crosses the wall $\mathfrak{d}_{1}$ with multiplicity $a_{\infty}$ and the wall $\mathfrak{d}_{(i-1)/i}$ with multiplicity $a_{i-1}-(2a_{i}-a_{i+1})$ .

#### Theorem 7.6.

If $2a\leq h-1$ , the map $\varphi$ is a $q$ -weighted bijection from $\CP(h-1,h,b,a)$ to $\BL_{+}(h,h-1,b,a)$ .

#### Proof.

The proof follows similarly to that of 6.18, since the map $\varphi$ is still defined by taking successive applications of the map $\ttheta$ and extracting the associated quantum binomial coefficient. One can obtain a quantum recursion for the compatible pairs using 7.3 and 7.4 that matches the recursion given for broken lines of positive angular momentum given in 5.9. Thus, we can conclude that $\varphi$ is a bijection that preserves quantum weights. ∎

### 7.2. The theta basis element with initial exponent $(m,m)$

The only elements of the theta basis in $\mathcal{A}_{q}(2,2)$ that are not cluster monomials are the theta functions $\vartheta_{Q,(m,m)}$ (where $Q$ is a generic point in the first quadrant). In contrast to the cluster monomial case, a quantum weighting for the corresponding compatible pairs on $\mathcal{P}(m,m)$ has not yet been constructed. We begin by defining such a quantization. This quantization is defined recursively, rather than as a sum over pairs of edges as in Rupel’s quantization. This definition is convenient for our recursive approach to the bijection, though we expect that a more natural generalization of Rupel’s quantization can be formulated.

The quantum weighting will be defined recursively using the map $\theta$ between compatible pairs constructed by Lee–Li–Zelevinsky (see 6.5 for the definition). Note that we use the map $\theta$ rather than $\ttheta$ because the statement in 3.9 fails for the Dyck path $\mathcal{P}(m,m)$ . This recursion involves choosing a term of a quantum binomial coefficient according to the image of a compatible pair under $\theta$ .

The quantum binomial coefficient $\binom{h}{k}_{q}$ is naturally viewed as a sum over size- $k$ subsets of $[h]$ of monomial terms, i.e, $\binom{h}{k}_{q}=q^{c}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}J\subseteq[h]//|J|=k\end{subarray}}q^{2\sum_{j\in J}j}$ for some constant $c=c(h,k)$ . Given a size- $k$ subset $J\subseteq[h]$ , let $\binom{[h]}{J}_{q}$ denote the exponent of the monomial corresponding to $J$ in $\binom{h}{k}_{q}$ .

#### Definition 7.7.

The quantum weight $w_{q}(S_{1},S_{2})$ of a compatible pair $(S_{1},S_{2})$ on $\mathcal{P}(m,m)$ can be determined recursively as follows:

As a base case, we set $w_{q}(\mathcal{P}_{1},\emptyset)=0$ .

Let $U=\mathcal{P}_{1}\cut\sh(S_{2})=\{\eta_{i_{1}},\dots,\eta_{i_{h}}\}$ be the set of horizontal edges that are not in the shadow of $S_{2}$ , where $i_{1}<\cdots<i_{h}$ . Then $U\cut S_{1}=\{\eta_{i_{j}}:j\in J\}$ for some $J\subseteq\{1,\dots,h\}$ . We then set

$$ w_{q}(S_{1},S_{2})=w_{q}(S_{1}^{\prime},S_{2}^{\prime})+\binom{[h]}{J}_{q^{4}}\,, $$

where $(S_{1}^{\prime},S_{2}^{\prime})=\theta(S_{1},S_{2})$ .

Note that, if $(S_{1}^{\prime},S_{2}^{\prime})=\theta(S_{1},S_{2})$ , then $|S_{1}^{\prime}|\geq\min(m,|S_{1}|+1)$ and $|S_{2}^{\prime}|\leq\max(0,|S_{2}|-1)$ . Thus, any compatible pair is sent to $(\mathcal{P}_{1},\emptyset)$ under finitely many applications of $\theta$ , so 7.7 is well-defined.

Using the quantum weighting, we can construct a map from compatible pairs to broken lines that respects quantum weights. Let $(S_{1}^{(i)},S_{2}^{(i)})=\underbrace{\theta\circ\cdots\circ\theta}_{i}(S_{1},S_{2})$ .

#### Definition 7.8.

Let $\varphi:\CP(m,m,a,b)\to\BL_{-}(m,m,a,b)$ be the map taking the compatible pair $(S_{1},S_{2})$ to the broken line that bending at the wall $\mathfrak{d}_{(\ell-1)/\ell}$ with multiplicity $h+|S_{2}^{(\ell+1)}|-2|S_{2}^{(\ell)}|-|S_{1}^{(\ell)}|$ .

#### Theorem 7.9.

If $2b\leq m$ , the map $\varphi:\CP(m,m,a,b)\to\BL_{-}(m,m,a,b)$ is a $q$ -weighted bijection.

#### Proof.

The size of the set $J$ in applying 7.7 to the compatible pair $(S_{1}^{(\ell)},S_{2}^{(\ell)})$ is precisely $h+|S_{2}^{(\ell+1)}|-2|S_{2}^{(\ell)}|-|S_{1}^{(\ell)}|$ . Thus, the binomial coefficient factor that a broken line attains by bending at the wall $\mathfrak{d}_{(\ell-1)/\ell}$ is the same as the binomial coefficient in 7.7 attained by applying $\theta$ to the set of corresponding compatible pairs. ∎

Note that the positive angular momentum case is symmetric to the negative angular momentum case by reflecting the scattering diagram along the line $y=x$ . As a result of the bijectivity of $\varphi$ , we obtain an expansion formula in terms of compatible pairs for the quantum theta basis element $\theta_{(m,m),q}$ .

#### Theorem 7.10.

The theta basis element $\vartheta_{Q,(m,m)}$ in $\mathcal{A}_{q}(2,2)$ is given by

$$ \vartheta_{Q,(m,m)}=\sum_{(S_{1},S_{2})}q^{w_{q}(S_{1},S_{2})}X_{1}^{-m+r|S_{2}|}X_{2}^{-m+r|S_{1}|}\,, $$

where the sum ranges over all compatible pairs on $\mathcal{P}(m,m)$ .

#### Proof.

By definition, the theta function $\vartheta_{Q,(m,m)}$ can be expressed as a sum over broken lines. Using 7.9, the expansion formula in terms of compatible pairs follows directly by applying the bijection $\varphi$ to the corresponding broken lines. ∎

### 7.3. Equivalence of bases for the quantum Kronecker cluster algebra

Lastly, we show that, for the quantum Kronecker cluster algebra, the quantum theta basis coincides with a number of other bases. The bases we consider are

- (1) the quantum bracelets basis [30, Definition 4.9],

- (2) the quantum theta basis [9, Proposition 3.1]*,

- (3) the basis $\mathcal{B}$ consisting of the quantum cluster monomials and $\{z_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}$ in [10, Definition 3.4],

- (4) the quantum triangular basis [3, Theorem 1.4], and

- (5) the quantum greedy basis [18, Theorem 9].

The following discussion concerns only the quantum Kronecker cluster algebra, though these bases may coincide in a more general setting. All bases mentioned contain the cluster monomials, so it is enough to show that the remaining elements coincide.

The fact that (1) and (2) coincide is due to the recent work of Mandel and Qin [25, Theorem 1.4], who showed that the theta and bracelets bases coincide in a much more general setting.

To show that (2) and (3) coincide, it is enough to check that (the specialization of) $\vartheta_{Q,(1,-1,0,0)}$ and $z_{1}$ are equal. This is because the $z_{n}$ ’s satisfy the Chebyshev recursion of the first kind by definition, while Mandel and Qin [25, Example 5.8] showed that the same recursion holds for the theta functions $\vartheta_{Q,(n,-n,0,0)}$ . By comparing [6, Lemma 3.3] and [25, Lemma 8.4], it is readily seen that $z_{1}=\vartheta_{Q,(1,-1,0,0)}|_{y_{1}=y_{2}=1}$ .

The bases (3) and (4) can be shown to coincide by recent work of Li [23, Theorem 1.2] which determine the support of triangular basis elements for skew-symmetric rank- $2$ quantum cluster algebras. It is then straightforward to check that the supports of the elements $z_{n}$ are equal to the supports of the non-cluster-monomial elements in the triangular basis, so the bases coincide.

We can then show that (3) and (5) coincide by directly verifying that the elements $z_{n}$ satisfy the recursion given in [18, Theorem 7], which characterizes the greedy basis. We do so using the Laurent expansion of $z_{n}$ given by the work of Ding-Xu. It follows directly from [10, Proposition 4.4] that $z_{n}=s_{n}-s_{n-2}$ , where $s_{n}$ is the element

$$ s_{n}=\sum_{p+r\leq n}\binom{n-r}{p}_{q}\binom{n-p}{r}_{q}q^{-(2p-n)(2r-n)}X_{1}^{2p-n}X_{2}^{2r-n}\,. $$

This is a special case of the $q$ -analogue of the following lemma, which can be easily proved by the standard generating function method.

#### Lemma 7.12.

For any nonnegative integers $n,p,r$ with $p\geq r$ , we have

$$ \sum_{k=0}^{p}(-1)^{k}\binom{n-1-r}{p-k}P(k)\binom{n-2r+k-1}{k}=0, $$

where $P(x)$ is any polynomial in $x$ of degree $\leq r-1$ .

#### Remark 7.13.

We note that the basis consisting of the cluster monomials and $\{s_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}$ that appears in the work of Çanakçı and Lampe [6, Definition 4.15]* is not identical to these other bases. It instead coincides (after specializing and possibly reordering the principal coefficients) with the basis $\mathcal{S}$ from the work of Ding-Xu [10, Definition 3.4]. The elements $s_{n}$ are related to the elements $z_{n}$ in the basis $\mathcal{B}$ , and their Laurent expansion is given in Equation 7.11. The work of Çanakçı and Lampe was later generalized to quantum cluster algebras from unpunctured orbifolds by Min Huang [16].
